title: Testing overview: faults, failures and test design
summary: Why we test, what a fault and a failure are, the levels of testing, black-box versus white-box, and the three ingredients of every test design.

sections.heading: Introduction
paras: Nobody is perfect, and large systems are guaranteed to contain mistakes. The purpose of testing is to find as many of those mistakes as possible before users do. A compiler catches syntax errors for you, but it cannot catch logic errors: code that compiles fine yet computes the wrong thing.

Testing means deliberately trying to make the software fail, then tracing each failure back to the fault that caused it so it can be fixed (debugged). If your tests never trigger a failure, you have learned nothing; a good test suite is one that would catch faults if they were there.

sections.heading: Faults and failures
paras: A fault (also called a defect or bug) is a mistake in code or documentation, such as writing * instead of / in a temperature conversion. A failure is an event where the software does not meet its goals: a wrong value, a crash, a freeze, or incorrect behaviour.

One fault can cause several different failures, one fault may never cause a failure at all (if you are lucky), and several faults in combination can cause a failure. This is why a single passing run proves little, and why you need many small, repeatable test cases rather than one big trial.

sections.heading: Levels of testing
paras: Testing happens at several scales. This unit focuses on unit testing: testing individual components or submodules in isolation. Larger scales build on it: integration testing checks combined modules, system testing checks the whole product, and acceptance, performance and installation testing check it against user and environment needs. Regression testing re-runs old tests after every change to make sure a fix did not break something else.

sections.heading: Black-box versus white-box
paras: In black-box testing you design test cases from the submodule specification alone: what it is supposed to do, not how it is coded. You do not need to see the code, so testers with less programming knowledge can do it. In white-box (clear-box) testing you design cases by analysing paths through the actual production code. White-box can pick up defects black-box misses, but white-box tests usually need updating whenever the production code changes. This unit teaches both: black-box first, white-box later.

sections.heading: Designing tests: cases, data, expected results
paras: Every test design has the same three ingredients. First, list the test cases: each distinct situation or category of behaviour the unit must handle. Second, pick test data for each case: concrete inputs the unit will receive. Third, calculate the expected result for each case: the exact output you demand. If you cannot say what the right answer is, you cannot verify anything.

Two engineering habits make tests trustworthy. Repeatability: the same test must give the same outcome every time until the software itself changes, otherwise a pass or fail tells you nothing. Automation: test code runs with no human in the loop (all inputs hard-coded), so the whole suite can be re-run after every change. Agile teams push this further with test-driven development (TDD): write the test cases first, so the tests embody the requirements and keep the project on track without a heavyweight specification.
bullets: One test case checks one thing and gives one pass or fail verdict.
Many small cases isolate faults faster than one giant case.
Never mix production code and test code: keep them in separate files.
Test code often equals or exceeds production code in volume; that is normal.

callout.text: If asked to contrast fault and failure, give both definitions plus the three relations: one fault can cause several failures, one fault may never cause a failure, and several faults combined can cause one failure.

recall.q: What is the difference between a fault and a failure?
recall.a: A fault is a mistake in code or docs (e.g. * instead of /); a failure is an event where the software misses its goals (wrong output, crash). Testing causes failures so you can trace back to faults and debug them.

recall.q: What are the three ingredients of every test design?
recall.a: List the test cases (one per behaviour category), pick test data per case, and calculate the expected result per case. Without a known expected result you cannot verify anything.

recall.q: Why must tests be repeatable and automated?
recall.a: Repeatability means the same outcome until the software changes, so a fail-then-pass proves the fix worked. Automation (no user input, hard-coded data) makes re-running the whole suite cheap after every change.

citations.locator: PDF pp. 6-10 (Why testing; faults vs failures)
citations.excerpt: Testing is finding logic errors: code that is syntactically correct but computes the wrong thing. A fault is a mistake in code or docs; a failure is an event where the software fails to meet its goals.

citations.locator: PDF pp. 11-18 (Unit testing concepts; repeatability, automation, TDD)
citations.excerpt: Unit testing means testing individual components: design, implement and execute test cases. Test code is kept separate from production code; tests must be repeatable and automated. In TDD, test cases are written first and embody the requirements.

citations.locator: PDF pp. 19-22 (Black vs white box; you cannot test everything)
citations.excerpt: Black-box tests are designed from the specification alone; white-box tests are designed by analysing paths through production code. Exhaustive testing is impossible (a 32-bit int already has 4 billion values), so a small set must cover as much behaviour as possible.

activities.prompt: One fault always causes exactly one failure.
activities.confirm: One fault can cause several failures, or none at all.
activities.explanation: Faults and failures are many-to-many: one fault can trigger several different failures, a fault may never trigger any, and several faults can combine into one failure.

activities.prompt: Which testing level checks an individual component in isolation?

distractor.1: System testing checks the whole product, not one unit.
distractor.2: Acceptance checks user needs, much later.
distractor.3: Regression re-runs old tests after changes.

activities.explanation: Unit testing targets individual components or submodules; the larger scales (integration, system, acceptance) build on top of it.

visuals.title: From fault to fix: the testing loop
visuals.what: Testing deliberately triggers failures, traces them to faults, and verifies the fix by re-running.
visuals.caption: Each failure is a clue. The loop only closes when the same test passes after the fix.
visuals.alt: Diagram with nodes for fault, failure, debug and re-test in a loop.

visuals.title: Black-box versus white-box
visuals.what: Same goal, different source of test cases: the specification versus the code.
visuals.caption: Black-box is stable across rewrites; white-box sees what black-box can only guess.
visuals.alt: Side-by-side comparison of black-box and white-box testing.
visuals.why: Pick black-box for early, stable tests; add white-box when the code hides decisions the spec never mentions.
